name: Argireline

lead: Argireline (acetyl hexapeptide-8) is a short synthetic peptide applied to soften the look of expression lines, especially on the forehead and around the eyes. It is often marketed as a needle-free or botox-like alternative.

It is modelled on part of SNAP-25, a protein that botulinum toxin type A also targets, and is proposed to compete with it in the SNARE complex, slightly reducing neurotransmitter release and muscle contraction. Published human studies are small and short, some reporting reduced measured wrinkle depth over about four weeks. A 2025 review notes its passage through the skin barrier is limited and that no study has compared it directly with botulinum toxin.

paras: It is applied as a serum or eye cream once or twice daily, often as part of a multi-ingredient anti-aging routine, and judged over several weeks. Effects reported are far milder than injected toxin.
It is generally well tolerated and sold as a cosmetic. Skin penetration is reported to be limited, so real-world results vary.

angle.text: Users apply Argireline as a needle-free alternative to Botox for forehead lines and crow's feet. The peptide imitates part of a protein botulinum toxin targets, to slightly dampen the muscle signal behind expression lines. Studies are small and short, and how much reaches the muscle is debated.

lead: Argireline, the trade name of acetyl hexapeptide-8 (originally labelled acetyl hexapeptide-3), is a synthetic six-amino-acid peptide used as a topical cosmetic ingredient intended to soften the appearance of expression lines, particularly around the eyes and forehead [1][2]. It is a short fragment modelled on SNAP-25, a protein that is also a target of botulinum toxin type A, and it is often described in marketing as a "botox-like" or needle-free alternative [1][3].

The proposed mechanism is that the peptide competes with SNAP-25 in assembling the SNARE complex, which would modestly reduce neurotransmitter release at the neuromuscular junction and therefore muscle contraction [3][4]. A 2025 review notes that, because the peptide is large and water-loving, its passage through the outer skin barrier is limited and its ability to reach the neuromuscular junction remains uncertain [3].

Published human data consist mainly of small, short studies, several of them linked to manufacturers or conducted with the ingredient inside multi-component formulations. Some report reductions in measured wrinkle depth over about four weeks, while reviewers describe inconsistent statistical significance and note that no study has directly compared the peptide with botulinum toxin [1][3][5].
infobox: Acetyl hexapeptide-8, acetyl hexapeptide-3 (older INCI name)
Cosmetic ingredient; not an approved drug for wrinkles

paras: Acetyl hexapeptide-8 is used in serums, creams and eye products marketed for lines on the forehead and around the eyes, and appears in some formulations for scars, skin elasticity and hydration [1][3]. It is commonly combined with other actives such as hyaluronic acid, and a US drug-label listing shows it as one of several peptides in a product marketed for stretch marks [6][6].

A small number of studies have explored it outside cosmetics. A pilot randomised trial examined topical acetyl hexapeptide-8 alongside botulinum toxin injections in people with blepharospasm (involuntary eyelid spasm), and a 2023 report described polydioxanone threads loaded with the peptide as a controlled-release system for facial lifting [7][8].

The original 2002 report by the developing group described a 10 percent peptide emulsion that reduced wrinkle depth by up to 30 percent over 30 days on skin-topography analysis in healthy women volunteers, alongside laboratory findings that the peptide reduced neurotransmitter release with lower efficacy than botulinum toxin [9]. Later work by other groups reported similar directions of effect in small samples [10][11].

Wikipedia's summary, drawing on a 2025 review, states that results have been mixed in statistical significance, that outcome measures vary between studies, and that better results tend to appear when the peptide is part of multi-ingredient products, which makes its individual contribution hard to isolate [1][3]. A 2024 systematic review of cosmeceuticals graded the evidence for peptides, including argireline, relatively highly, though that review addresses peptides as a class rather than testing argireline against botulinum toxin [12].

Skin penetration is a recurring theme. In vitro work found that very little applied peptide crossed the outer skin layer, and research groups have explored emulsion design, chemical modification of the peptide, iontophoresis, microneedles and transferosomes as ways to improve delivery [3][13][14][15][16].

A randomised, placebo-controlled study in 60 Chinese adults applied argireline or placebo (3:1 allocation) to periorbital wrinkles twice daily for four weeks. The authors reported a total anti-wrinkle efficacy of 48.9 percent in the argireline group versus 0 percent for placebo on subjective grading, with improvements in silicone-replica analysis and no notable adverse events [10]. A registered phase 3 trial of argireline for periorbital wrinkles (about 70 participants, started 2009) is listed on ClinicalTrials.gov [17].

A 2023 double-blind randomised trial compared an acetyl hexapeptide-3 cream with a palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 cream for crow's feet, and a 2023 study used a camera-based skin analysis system to assess an argireline-containing hyaluronic acid serum on surface wrinkles [18][19]. A 2019 Korean study examined a hyaluronic acid microneedle patch containing acetyl hexapeptide-8 and epidermal growth factor, so effects there cannot be attributed to the peptide alone [20].

In blepharospasm, a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 24 patients receiving botulinum toxin injections found a non-significant trend toward longer symptom control with daily topical acetyl hexapeptide-8 (3.7 versus 3.0 months), with no significant adverse events; the authors called it promising and safe [7]. Other registered trials on ClinicalTrials.gov include a small oily-skin study and a terminated blepharospasm study [21][22][23].

The peptide corresponds to residues 12 to 17 of SNAP-25. It is proposed to interfere with formation of the ternary SNARE complex needed for calcium-dependent vesicle fusion, thereby lowering release of neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine [3][9]. Experiments cited in the original paper reported that it inhibited release with potency comparable to botulinum toxin A in cell assays but lower maximal efficacy [9].

Because of its molecular weight of about 889 Da and hydrophilicity, the peptide has limited passage through the stratum corneum. A 2015 in vitro study of a commercial emulsion reported that under 0.2 percent of the applied peptide was recovered beyond the outer layer, with most removed by washing [1][13]. Another group reported that vehicle composition changes delivery to the skin [14]. A 2018 study of chemically modified analogues reported improved in vitro permeation for some variants [15].

The original investigators reported no oral toxicity or primary irritation at high doses in their tests, and clinical studies to date report few adverse events [9][10]. A cell-culture study of cytotoxicity and a 2026 chicken-embryo study of neurodevelopmental responses to argireline and another peptide are among the laboratory safety investigations; the latter authors describe it as indicating teratogenic potential in that model, and no human data address pregnancy [24][25]. Product labels for peptide creams typically advise external use only and avoiding the eyes [6].

Acetyl hexapeptide-8 has the sequence Ac-Glu-Glu-Met-Gln-Arg-Arg-NH2 with an acetylated N-terminus and amidated C-terminus, a design that is described as protecting it from enzymatic breakdown [1][2]. It was developed by the Barcelona company Lipotec and launched in 2001 as the first cosmetic peptide aimed at neurotransmitter release; Lubrizol acquired Lipotec in 2012 and markets Argireline [1][2]. The name acetyl hexapeptide-3 was an earlier cosmetic-ingredient label that Wikipedia describes as incorrect for the amide form [1].
A 2024 analysis of US Google search volume found growing public interest in the ingredient over the 2013 to 2023 decade [26].

Argireline is widely sold as a cosmetic ingredient and is a standard example in discussions of "botox alternative" skincare. Reviewers distinguish between its proposed mechanism and the evidence of effect in people, and some commentary frames needle-free delivery as an unresolved analytical and formulation challenge [3][27].

timeline.event: Lipotec launches Argireline as a cosmetic peptide [2].
Developers publish the first report of antiwrinkle activity in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science [9].
A randomised placebo-controlled study in Chinese adults and a pilot blepharospasm trial are published [7][10].
In vitro studies report limited skin penetration from cosmetic formulations [13][14].
A review of permeability and efficacy describes inconsistent significance across studies [3].
